title: Power of two, or not?
prompt:
A power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, and so on) has exactly one bit set. Subtracting 1 clears that bit and sets every bit below it, so `n` and `n - 1` share no set bits and `n & (n - 1)` is zero. Any other positive number keeps its highest set bit through the subtraction, so the AND is not zero.

The starter reads a 64-bit number into `n_r` and always prints that it is not a power of two. Point `x0` at `fmt_yes` instead when `n_r` is a power of two: compute `n - 1` in a spare register and test the two with `tst`, which sets the flags from their AND.

Watch zero and the negative numbers: the bit test alone gets one of each wrong.

## what is checked

- `64 is a power of two` for the sample input
- the program exits cleanly
- the bits are tested with `tst`
- the right answer for other numbers, including 0, 1, a number wider than 32 bits, and negative numbers
starter:
// decide whether a number is a power of two
define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)

define(n_r, x19)

.data
fmt_num:    .string "%ld"
fmt_yes:    .string "%ld is a power of two\n"
fmt_no:     .string "%ld is not a power of two\n"

.bss
.balign 8
n_m:        .skip 8

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        ldr     x0, =fmt_num                // read n into n_m
        ldr     x1, =n_m
        bl      scanf
        ldr     x9, =n_m
        ldr     n_r, [x9]

        ldr     x0, =fmt_no                 // placeholder: always says no

        // TODO: point x0 at fmt_yes instead when n is a power of two.

        mov     x1, n_r
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

hiddenCases.stdout: 0 is not a power of two
96 is not a power of two
4294967297 is not a power of two
-8 is not a power of two
-9223372036854775808 is not a power of two
